items.title: [climatechangenews.com] COP17 urges subsidy cuts as nature finance gap persists before COP31
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

Forbes cited national figures showing that power plants serving data centers consumed far more water in 2023 than data centers used for cooling.

items.title: [eos.org] Antarctic grass and pearlwort show opposite responses to experimental warming
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A seven-year field experiment on King George Island found that Antarctica’s only two native flowering plants responded in opposite ways to warming: Antarctic hair grass showed reduced water flow through its leaves and lower photosynthesis, while Antarctic pearlwort showed increases in both. The findings come from plants grown in open-top chambers near Poland’s Henryk Arctowski Antarctic Station. The chambers produced sharp temperature swings, not just higher average temperatures: during the 2018–19 summer, plants inside spent far more time below freezing than those outside. Researchers are now examining plants that have remained in the chambers for 16 years, along with microorganisms living around them.

The findings come from plants grown in open-top chambers near Poland’s Henryk Arctowski Antarctic Station. The chambers produced sharp temperature swings, not just higher average temperatures: during the 2018–19 summer, plants inside spent far more time below freezing than those outside. Researchers are now examining plants that have remained in the chambers for 16 years, along with microorganisms living around them (eos.org, zmescience.com). Freeze exposure: In the 2018–19 summer, chamber plants spent 309 hours below freezing, compared with 32 hours in nearby open plots (eos.org, zmescience.com). Leaf changes: Chamber-grown grass developed narrower water-carrying vessels and thicker leaves, while pearlwort formed wider vessels and more elastic cells (eos.org, zmescience.com). Freeze-count threshold: Peter Convey, a polar terrestrial ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey, said 0°C may be too high a threshold for counting freezing events because many soil microbes and small invertebrates remain active down to about −2°C (eos.org, zmescience.com).

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Swedish survey finds valuable meadows stable, but upkeep remains essential
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Sweden’s valuable meadows and grazing lands have largely retained their natural and cultural value, according to an analysis by the Swedish Board of Agriculture. Of 300,000 hectares identified as valuable, 260,000 had been fully inventoried. In 2020, nearly 70% of that fully inventoried area — 175,000 hectares — received environmental management payments, 8,000 hectares more than in 2018. Repeat surveys conducted 10 to 20 years apart found that most inventoried sites remained meadows or pastures. Some sites lost value when left unmanaged and became overgrown, while restoration helped recover value elsewhere. The agency says continued inventories are needed to track changes.

items.content_html:

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Liberals defeat Conservative bill to repeal B.C. tanker ban
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Canada’s Liberal government defeated a Conservative bill Wednesday to repeal the oil tanker ban on British Columbia’s northern coast, leaving the restrictions in place. The law bars tankers from carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil in the covered coastal area. Conservatives cited Calgary-based Strathcona Resources’ proposal to move as many as 250,000 barrels of oil a day by rail through Prince Rupert for export. Prime Minister Mark Carney agreed with British Columbia earlier this summer to maintain the ban. He and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith subsequently announced a proposed pipeline route to the south that would comply with it. Smith supported repeal. The bill’s defeat at second reading means it will not proceed to committee.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Data-center construction is creating union jobs in Nevada, while automation cuts or threatens positions in hospitality and customer service and employers in other sectors increase output without expanding headcount. A report by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found little evidence of widespread AI-related job losses in the state so far, while a survey of Swiss finance chiefs found 64% expect fewer entry-level finance jobs over the next three years. In Nevada, self-driving vehicles, casino robots and digital guest services are changing work on the Las Vegas Strip as thousands of tradespeople build data centers near Reno. items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Legombang Treehouse reinterprets traditional Balinese architecture as a contemporary tropical family home, using reclaimed timber, passive design, and a treehouse-like structure woven around the site's existing trees. Designed by Cave Urban co-founder Jed Long for his own family, the house is located in Pantai Lembeng, Ketewel, Bali. As both architect and client, Jed had the opportunity to explore his own approach to tropical family living without the constraints of a conventional client brief.
